883.title: George Herbert
883.hook: a country parson poet: Love bade me welcome, yet my soul drew back
883.howItsDone: Herbert's poems are read in Anglican and other churches, and several have become hymns; the Church of England remembers him each year with a commemoration in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The King James Bible, made for the ear. Your line was the language of heaven, in english. Which old Bible phrase did you catch in ordinary talk? Day eight hundred eighty-three.

A guest stands at an open door. The host says come in, you're welcome. And the guest hangs back on the step. Muddy shoes. Empty hands. Not sure about a place at this table. That small, stubborn hanging back is the whole subject of a short poem by an English country parson. It begins: "Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back". The parson, the story goes, was a gifted man who could have had a career at court, and chose instead a small parish and a life of writing poems that, tradition says, he wasn't even sure anyone should read. Today: George Herbert.

George Herbert was a priest in the Church of England, serving a country parish. His poems were gathered in a book called The Temple, published after his death. The story goes that he sent the manuscript to a friend, asking him to publish it if it might help some troubled soul, and to burn it if not. The friend published it. The last poem in one part of the book is called Love, and it's a conversation at a door. Love invites the speaker in. The speaker draws back, feeling guilty of dust and sin. Love, quick-eyed, notices, and comes closer, asking gently if anything is lacking. A guest worthy to be here, the speaker answers. Love says: you will be. The speaker objects again: I'm unkind and ungrateful, I can't even look at you. Love takes his hand and smiles: who made the eyes but I? Then the speaker tries one last way out. If he can't be a guest, he'll work. He'll serve the meal. And Love says no: sit down, and taste my meat. The poem ends with six plain words: "So I did sit and eat." No speech. No grand conversion. Just a person who finally stops arguing and accepts the seat. Some readers hear the Lord's Supper in it, Holy Communion. Others hear the banquet of heaven, or simply the shape of grace. Either way, the struggle is the same: it can be harder to be welcomed than to be useful. Herbert's poem lets Love win the argument by being kind.

Here's the practice: read Love, the poem. If you can, find George Herbert's Love, the third poem of that name, and read it slowly, all the way through. If you can't look it up, hold just its first line and its last: love bade me welcome. So I did sit and eat. Then sit. Notice where you hang back from being welcomed: by a person, by rest, by God if you believe in God. If you pray, you can simply accept the seat. If you don't, just practice sitting, without earning it. The bell holds the time.
George Herbert. An English country parson whose poem Love tells of a soul that draws back from welcome, argues, tries to serve instead, and finally sits down and eats.
Your line: love bade me welcome. Today, when someone offers you something, a seat, a meal, a kind word, try simply taking it, without arguing or paying it back. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

884.title: John Donne
884.hook: a poet-dean: no man is an island; any man's death diminishes me
884.howItsDone: Donne's words are read at funerals and memorial services, and in some parishes a bell is still tolled for the dead, with prayers for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Herbert, and a soul that finally sat down to eat. Your line was love bade me welcome. Did you manage to take something offered, without paying it back? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

A man lies sick in bed in London, too ill to get up. Through the window comes the sound of a church bell, tolling slowly, the way a passing bell rang when someone in the parish was dying. He doesn't know who it's for. Instead of finding out, he picks up the thought and turns it over, and writes. That sick man was a poet who had once written daring love poems, and who became a priest and the dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London. Out of that sickbed came a few lines that still turn up far from any church. Today: John Donne.

Donne wrote his Devotions during a serious illness, as a series of meditations, prayers and arguments with himself about sickness, death and God. In one of them he hears the bell, and first wonders whether it's tolling for someone he doesn't know, or, if he's sicker than he thinks, for himself. Then comes the passage, here in modern spelling: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main". The main is the mainland. A little later he says: "any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind". And he ends with this: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." Donne is using the word man the way his century did, for every human being. That's why today's line says it plainly: no one is an island. His point isn't just that people are connected in a pleasant way. It's sharper than that. In his view, a stranger's death actually takes something from each of us, because we're part of the same body of humankind. Some readers hear Paul behind it. Paul describes the church as one body with many parts, in the King James Bible: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." Donne stretched that body wide. Every bell, every funeral, every name in the news is, in his picture, a clod of earth washed away by the sea.

Here's the practice: notice how connected you are. Start with something close: the chair under you, the clothes you're wearing, the last thing you ate. Ask quietly, who made this? Who grew it, sewed it, drove it here? Let the faces you'll never meet come to mind, one after another. Then follow one thread further back: the field, the factory, the ship. Breathe in, and feel yourself a piece of the continent. Breathe out. If you pray, you can hold them all before God for a moment. If you don't, just rest in being part of the main. The bell holds the time.
John Donne. A poet who became a priest and dean of St Paul's, who wrote from a sickbed that no one is an island, and that the tolling bell tolls for each of us.
Your line: no one is an island. Today, when you hear news of a stranger's death, pause for one breath before you scroll on, and let it count. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

885.title: The Pilgrims and the Puritans
885.hook: crossing the Atlantic for religious freedom; their story with Native peoples is honestly mixed
885.howItsDone: Congregational and other churches in New England trace their roots to the Pilgrims and Puritans, and some now hold services of remembrance and reconciliation with Wampanoag and other Native communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Donne, listening to a bell from his sickbed. Your line was no one is an island. Did a stranger's news stop you for a breath? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

A small, crowded ship called the Mayflower drops anchor off a cold coast in late autumn. At the heart of the group on board are English Christians who wanted to worship in their own way, without the Church of England telling them how. Many of them have already lived as exiles in Holland. Others on the ship came for land and work. Now they've crossed an ocean. The version told in school pageants ends with a shared harvest feast. The real story is longer, and harder, and it doesn't belong only to the people on the ship. It belongs just as much to the people who were already standing on that shore. Today: The Pilgrims and the Puritans.

First, two names that get mixed up. The Pilgrims were Separatists: they believed the Church of England was beyond fixing, so they left it. The Puritans, who came after them and settled around Boston, wanted to stay in the church and purify it from within. Both crossed the Atlantic for the freedom to worship as they believed God wanted. The Puritans' leader John Winthrop told his settlers they would be like a city upon a hill, with every eye on them. He was reaching for Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Now the people on the shore. The land around Plymouth was home to the Wampanoag. The Pilgrims' own governor, William Bradford, wrote that after a hard first winter, an English-speaking Native man named Squanto came to help them, showing them how to plant corn and where to fish, and that a peace was agreed with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit. Bradford also wrote that Squanto had learned English after being carried off from his home. That peace held for a time. Later generations broke it, in land taken and in war. And the Puritans who came for freedom punished or banished some who worshipped differently, as tomorrow's story shows. So the story is honestly mixed: real faith, real courage, real help received, and real harm done. Which is why today's line is a question: freedom for whom?

Here's the practice: learn whose land you're on. Wherever you're sitting, people lived on this ground before the town or city around you had its name. After the bell, you can look it up. For now, just sit with the ground under you. Feel the floor, the earth beneath the floor. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind the people who walked here first, whose names you may not know yet. If you pray, you can remember them before God. If you don't, simply hold them in respectful attention for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
The Pilgrims and the Puritans. English Christians who crossed the Atlantic for freedom to worship, whose story with the Native peoples already there holds both help and harm.

segments.voice: Your line: freedom for whom? Today, find out who lived on the land where you live before your town had its name, and say their name out loud once. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

886.title: Roger Williams
886.hook: banished from Massachusetts, he founds Rhode Island with freedom of conscience for all
886.howItsDone: Baptists and others in America honor Roger Williams as an early champion of religious liberty, and his idea of soul liberty is still taught in churches that hold to freedom of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Pilgrims and the Puritans, a story of real help and real harm. Your line was freedom for whom? Did you learn the name of the people whose land you're on? Day eight hundred eighty-six.

The court in Massachusetts has made its decision: the young minister must leave the colony. His crime isn't theft or violence. It's ideas. He's been saying that the government has no business punishing people for how they worship, and that the king's charter can't hand over land that belongs to the Native peoples who live on it. Tradition says he slipped away in winter, before they could ship him back to England, that Native people sheltered him, and that Narragansett leaders let him settle on their land. He went on to found a settlement where nobody would be punished for their conscience. He called it Providence. Today: Roger Williams.

Roger Williams was a Puritan himself, and an intense one. He wasn't arguing that faith didn't matter. He was arguing that it mattered too much to be forced. A belief pressed on someone at the point of a sword, in his view, isn't faith at all. He leaned on a parable of Jesus. A farmer sows good seed, and an enemy comes by night and sows weeds among the wheat. The servants want to pull the weeds out at once. The farmer says no, in the King James Bible: "lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest". For Williams, that settled it. Sorting true believers from false isn't a job for magistrates and courts. It's God's, at the harvest. Until then, let both grow. This freedom came to be called soul liberty: the freedom of each person's conscience before God, which no government should touch. He pictured a hedge or wall between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world, to protect the garden. And he lived it. His colony became a place where Baptists, Quakers and Jews could worship openly. He disagreed sharply with some of them, and said so in public debates, but he didn't drive them out. He also learned the Narragansett language and wrote a book about it, and insisted that land be bought from its people rather than simply taken. He wasn't a saint in a stained glass window. He could be prickly and stubborn. But the idea he was banished for traveled a long way.

Here's the practice: defend someone's right to disagree. Bring to mind a belief you think is wrong, about faith, politics, anything. Try putting it in one sentence the way someone who holds it would say it, fairly, with no sneer in it. Now, quietly, try saying to yourself: they have the right to believe this. Not that they're right. Just that the choice is theirs, between them and their conscience. Notice what happens as you say it. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can rest with the farmer's words: let both grow together until the harvest. If you don't, just let the other person stand, unharvested, in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Roger Williams. A Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts, who founded Providence as a place where no one would be punished for their conscience, a freedom that came to be called soul liberty.
Your line: soul liberty. Today, when someone disagrees with you, try saying out loud, you have every right to see it that way, and mean it. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: George Fox and the Quakers
887.hook: a shoemaker's apprentice hears there is one, even Christ Jesus, who can speak to your condition
887.howItsDone: In a traditional Quaker meeting for worship, Friends sit together in silence with no set sermon, and anyone who feels moved may stand and speak briefly before the silence returns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Roger Williams, banished into the winter, building a colony where conscience could be free. Your line was soul liberty. Did you stand up for someone's right to disagree with you? Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A young man in England has been put to work with a shoemaker. Something inside him is restless, and he goes looking for help. He walks from minister to minister, asking his questions. In his own journal he remembers one of them telling him, more or less, to take up tobacco and sing psalms. Another, he says, got angry when he stepped on the edge of a flower bed. Nobody can reach him. He wanders, fasts, walks alone in the fields with his Bible. His name is George Fox, and what happens next starts a movement that sits down together in silence. Today: George Fox and the Quakers.

Fox describes the moment plainly. When all his hopes in other people were gone, and he had nothing outside himself to help him, he heard a voice that said, in his journal's words, "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." And then: "my heart did leap for joy." Notice what the voice doesn't say. It doesn't hand him a new argument or a better minister. It says someone can speak to his condition: not the human condition in general, but his own, the exact shape of his restlessness. Fox came to believe that the light of Christ could reach any person directly, a shoemaker as much as a scholar, a woman as much as a man. That conviction shaped the people who gathered around him, who called themselves Friends. Others called them Quakers, and the name stuck. Their worship looks different from a church service. In a traditional Quaker meeting, people sit together in silence, with no set sermon. If someone feels moved to speak, they stand and speak, briefly, and then the quiet returns. The silence isn't empty. It's waiting. There's an old story behind that kind of waiting. In the Bible, the prophet Elijah stands on a mountain. A wind tears at the rocks, but God is not in the wind. Then an earthquake, then a fire, and God is not in them either. And after the fire, in the King James words, "a still small voice." Friends sit down expecting that voice could come to anyone in the room. Other Christians pray with set words, music and liturgy, and they too speak of God meeting them there.

Here's the practice: sit in silence, waiting. Not trying to clear your mind, not trying to make anything happen. Just sitting the way Friends sit, as if something might be said. Let your hands rest. Notice the sounds in the room and let them pass. If you pray, you can hold Fox's words loosely: someone can speak to my condition. If you don't, simply wait, and notice what rises in the quiet without chasing it. The bell holds the time.
George Fox and the Quakers. A restless seeker who heard that Christ could speak to his condition, and the Friends who gathered around him to wait together in silence.

segments.voice: Your line: speak to my condition. Today, take one minute somewhere quiet, a parked car, a stairwell, before you open your phone, and just wait. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

888.title: Bunyan in jail
888.hook: a tinker imprisoned for preaching dreams the story that becomes Pilgrim's Progress
888.howItsDone: Christians in different churches read The Pilgrim's Progress at home, aloud with children, or in study groups, following Christian's journey a few chapters at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Fox, the seeker who heard that someone could speak to his condition. Your line was speak to my condition. Did you find a quiet minute and simply wait? Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

John Bunyan mends pots and pans for a living. He's a tinker, with a tinker's hands and very little schooling. He also preaches, without a license from the Church of England, and in his England that's against the law. So he's arrested and put in the county jail in Bedford. He's told he can go home if he promises to stop preaching. He won't promise. So the months in a cell turn into years, and his family outside struggles without him. A man with a hammer and no pulpit now has neither. What he does have is time, and a pen. Today: Bunyan in jail.

Listen to how the book he's remembered for begins: "As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and, as I slept, I dreamed a dream." A den. Old editions carry a note in the margin saying what the den is: the gaol, the jail. From the very first sentence, the book hints that it was dreamed behind bars. The dream is The Pilgrim's Progress. In it, a man named Christian carries a heavy burden and sets out from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City. On the way he meets characters with names you can't forget: Evangelist, who points the way, Obstinate and Pliable, Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Faithful, Hopeful, Giant Despair in his castle. Bunyan writes plainly, and Bible phrases run all through his pages. Here's what makes the jail matter. Bunyan couldn't walk anywhere. So he wrote a book that is nothing but walking: roads, hills, sloughs, valleys, gates. The man who was stuck gave readers a journey. Long before him, the apostle Paul wrote letters from his chains. To the Philippians, from prison, Paul writes that what happened to him has "fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel." Bunyan seems to have believed something like that about his cell. The waiting wasn't wasted. It became the dream.
screen: `AS I SLEPT, I DREAMED A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write while you wait. Think of a place where you feel stuck right now, a job, a hospital room, a season of life that won't move. In the quiet, let one line come to you about it. Not a solution. A line, an image, the start of a story. Hold it. When the bell ends, write it down somewhere you'll find it again. If you pray, you can bring the stuck place to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Bunyan in jail. A tinker locked up for preaching, who dreamed a pilgrim's journey in his cell and wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.
Your line: the dream in the jail. Today, when you're stuck waiting, in traffic, on hold, in a line, use two minutes to write something, even one sentence. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

889.title: The burden rolls away
889.hook: in Bunyan's story, Christian's burden falls off at the cross and rolls into a tomb
889.howItsDone: Christians bring their burdens to God in different ways: in personal prayer, in confession or the sacrament of reconciliation, at the communion table, or by laying a written worry at the foot of a cross in some churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bunyan in jail, the tinker who dreamed a journey in a cell. Your line was the dream in the jail. Did you write something while you waited? Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A heavy backpack does something strange over a long hike. At first you feel every pound. Then you stop noticing, and you lean forward without knowing it, and your shoulders forget what it was like to be light. Only when you set it down do you realize how bent you'd become. Bunyan's pilgrim starts his journey like that. The first picture of him in the book is a man in rags with a great burden on his back, reading a book and crying out, What shall I do? He carries that weight through the slough, past the gate, mile after mile. Today, in the story, it finally comes off. Today: the burden rolls away.

Christian runs, with difficulty, up a road fenced with a wall on either side, to a place that rises a little. At the top stands a cross, and below it, a tomb. Here's how Bunyan tells it: "Just as Christian came up with the Cross, his burden loosed from off his shoulders, and fell from off his back, and began to tumble, and so continued to do, till it came to the mouth of the Sepulchre, where it fell in, and I saw it no more." Look at what Christian does in that sentence. Nothing. He doesn't untie the straps. He doesn't throw it off. He just arrives, and the burden loosens. Bunyan, a Protestant preacher, is picturing what he believed about grace: that what Christ did on the cross lifts a weight a person can't lift alone. And the burden goes into the sepulchre, which some readers take as Christ's own tomb, and the narrator never sees it again. Christian's response is the next thing in the story. He stands looking at the cross, amazed, and tears run down his cheeks. Then he says, "He hath given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death." Rest. That word reaches back to something Jesus says in Matthew's gospel: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians from different churches describe how that rest comes in different ways: through baptism and the sacraments, through faith, through confession, through a lifetime of being made new. Bunyan's picture is one man's dream of it. And the road doesn't end at the cross. Christian keeps walking, lighter now, and there's still a long way to go.

Here's the practice: set down one burden. Name one weight you've been carrying so long you've stopped noticing it. A grudge, a worry, a regret, a promise you can't keep. Breathe in, and feel where it sits in your body. Breathe out, and let your shoulders drop, as if the straps had loosened on their own. If you pray, you can bring that weight to the cross, or rest with Jesus' words: come unto me, and I will give you rest. If you don't, simply let it be set down for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The burden rolls away. In The Pilgrim's Progress, the moment at the cross when Christian's burden loosens by itself, tumbles into the tomb, and is seen no more.

Your line: the burden rolled away. Today, when you notice your shoulders creeping up toward your ears, let them drop, and remember the picture of a weight tumbling downhill. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Christian. you've carried this burden since the City of Destruction. you reach a cross on a little hill. what happens?
options: you work hard to untie it.
it loosens and rolls away by itself.
someone takes it from you and carries it for you.
fork.reveal: it loosens from his shoulders and tumbles into the tomb, and the narrator sees it no more.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice image of letting go of stress.
what it means: in Bunyan's story, Christian's burden falls off at the cross and rolls into a tomb, and he weeps for joy.
what a scholar hears: Christian does nothing to remove it; the burden loosens as he arrives, Bunyan's picture of grace.
